chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan and 'Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Yahya ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Azraq, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who enters into the sa'y (running) between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and runs three or four circuits, then the truthful one (al-Saduq) meets him and invites him to fulfill a need or to eat. He (peace be upon him) said, 'If he answers him, there is no harm.'

The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: And when he tawaf around the House seven times and sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah seven times, he trims the hair of his head from its sides, and from his two eyebrows, and from his beard, and he has released himself from everything he was in a state of ihram for.

key_terms.السَّعْي: Sa'y (ritual walking/running between Safa and Marwah)
key_terms.الصَّدُوق: Al-Saduq (The Truthful, often referring to the Angel of Death or a spiritual entity in this context)
key_terms.الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَة: Al-Safa and Al-Marwah (the two hills in Mecca)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on interrupting sa'y between Safa and Marwah during Hajj?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the permissibility of interrupting the *sa'y* (walking between Safa and Marwa) for a valid need, such as eating, without invalidating the ritual. It highlights the flexibility in Shia jurisprudence regarding minor disruptions during Hajj, while the concluding remark details the specific acts of *taqsir* (trimming hair) required to exit the state of *ihram* after completing the rites.
